keyVerseText: I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word כֶּשֶׂב (keseb) is etymologically related to כֶּבֶשׂ (kebes), indicating a lamb or young sheep, sometimes a ram just old enough to butt. The form כֶּשֶׂב appears to be a transposition of כֶּבֶשׂ, emphasizing the idea of a young sheep or lamb. This root sense highlights the tender, youthful nature of the animal, distinguishing it from older sheep and underscoring its innocence and value as livestock.
usageInScripture: The term כֶּשֶׂב occurs thirteen times in the Hebrew Bible, consistently referring to lambs or young sheep. Its translations include phrases like "among the sheep," "the lambs," and "a lamb," showing a focus on the animal as both property and sacrificial offering. The word is used in contexts of possession, sacrifice, and food, revealing its integral role in Israelite worship and daily life. This consistency underscores the lamb's significance as a valuable and often sacrificial animal in biblical culture.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כֶּשֶׂב as a young lamb enriches our grasp of biblical sacrifice and God's provision. The lamb symbolizes innocence and purity, qualities essential to the sacrificial system that points forward to Christ, the Lamb of God, who takes away sin. The repeated use of this term in sacrificial contexts highlights the importance of offering something precious and unblemished to God. This word reminds believers of the cost and grace embodied in Christ’s sacrifice, inviting reflection on the innocence and substitutionary nature of the Lamb who redeems us.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 30:32, the word כֶּשֶׂב appears in the context of Jacob describing his wages, emphasizing the selection of speckled and spotted sheep among the flock. The mention of lambs or young sheep here highlights the careful attention to the quality and characteristics of the animals involved. This word contributes to the verse by underscoring the value and distinctiveness of the livestock, which serves as a tangible measure of God's blessing and provision in Jacob’s agreement.
